newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Caputo blasts Argentina's Falkland "charm" policy.
newsitem.headline: Caputo blasts Argentina's Falkland "charm" policy.

text.p: Argentina's former foreign minister Dante Caputo said on Thursday the government's so-called "charm offensive" Falkland Islands policy meant Britain would probably keep the disputed South Atlantic territory forever.

Caputo, who held the job from 1983-89 under the Radical government of Raul Alfonsin, attacked current Foreign Minister Guido Di Tella for claiming that his policies had succeeded in overcoming islanders' hostility towards Argentina.

Argentina and Britain fought a brief but bloody war in 1982 in which about 1,000 soldiers, mostly Argentine, died. Argentina lost the war but maintains its claim to sovereignty over the remote islands that it calls the Malvinas.
"If you assess the Malvinas issue we have taken a major step backwards and Argentina was never further from regaining the islands," Caputo told local radio.

"It has meant that the British occupation of the islands has no cost in diplomatic or prestige terms. They will stay forever," said Caputo, who recently left the Radicals to join another opposition party, the centre-left Frepaso coalition.

Since Peronist President Carlos Menem came to power in 1989, he has resumed diplomatic ties with Britain, hosted visits by British royals and forged close trade links, while insisting he will win back the islands by the year 2000.

Di Tella's policy has included sending the islanders Christmas cards with photos of his family, books and video cassettes. Such gestures have attracted criticism at home and Di Tella himself admitted they had won little ground.
But Di Tella changed tack Wednesday, claiming on local radio that he had brought about a radical change in attitude among the islanders, but had also made the British nervous.

"I have no doubt whatsoever that the 'charm policy' has been a success," he said, adding that an accord with Britain on oil exploration in the South Atlantic signed last year was "the biggest advance in 170 years" of territorial dispute.
